title: Curvature-amplified angular localization of radially localized states
abstract: We study a continuum Schrödinger particle on a surface of constant curvature subject to a radial random potential and a weaker angle-dependent perturbation. Exact angular-momentum decomposition reduces the rotationally symmetric problem to independent one-dimensional random radial channels. A positive radial Lyapunov exponent distinguishes radial Anderson localization from the circular probability profile imposed by symmetry. Projection of a narrow radial mode produces a disordered one-dimensional ring. For angular disorder that is stationary in physical arc length, the ring localization length grows as the inverse square of the perturbation amplitude. Equating this length with the geodesic circumference yields a shell-breaking radius that grows algebraically in flat space but as $2a\ln(1/\varepsilon)+O(1)$ on a hyperbolic surface of curvature radius $a$ and angular-disorder amplitude $\varepsilon$. Transfer-matrix and finite-ring calculations determine the crossover coefficient. Direct polar-grid calculations at the same angular energy as the ring model use unbiased tracking of the degenerate angular-momentum subspace across six independent radial-disorder realizations and quantify the validity of the single-mode projection. The noncommuting weak-disorder and flat-curvature limits establish a curvature-amplified crossover for this deliberately anisotropic disorder ensemble, rather than a generic metal--insulator transition on the hyperbolic plane.
summary: This paper analyzes the angular localization of quantum states on curved surfaces subjected to random potentials. The core finding is that the characteristic length scale at which the system transitions from being governed by radial confinement to angular confinement depends critically on the manifold's curvature. This leads to a distinct logarithmic scaling law on hyperbolic planes compared to flat space.
main_problem: The study investigates how angular localization of radially localized quantum states is amplified by the curvature of the underlying manifold, distinguishing this effect from generic metal-insulator transitions.
main_result: The crossover radius at which shell breaking occurs exhibits a distinct functional dependence on curvature: algebraic in flat space but logarithmic ($\propto 2a\ln(1/\varepsilon)$) on hyperbolic surfaces.
method: The authors employ exact angular-momentum decomposition, transfer-matrix calculations, and direct polar-grid simulations to analyze the localization length in both radial and angular directions.
model_or_system: The system is a continuum Schrödinger particle moving on a 2D Riemannian surface of constant curvature $K$, subjected to a dominant radial random potential ($V_r$) and a weaker, angle-dependent perturbation ($\varepsilon V_\perp$).
key_observables: Radial Lyapunov exponent ($\gamma_r$), angular localization length ($\xi_	heta$), shell-breaking radius ($r^*$), and the single-state normalized shell-extension indicator ($Q_{sh}$).
important_parameters: Gaussian curvature $K$, curvature radius $a$, radial disorder width $W_r$, and angular perturbation amplitude $\varepsilon$.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on separating genuine asymptotic localization from finite-size crossovers, and the derived crossover law is specific to this deliberately anisotropic disorder ensemble.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the geometry and localization mechanisms. Figure 2(a) compares Born approximation and transfer-matrix results for $\gamma_r$. Figure 9 plots the weak-disorder coefficient vs. $\ln(1/\epsilon)$ and derives the crossover radius $r^*/a$ based on curvature.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing radial localization via Lyapunov exponents in the symmetry limit ($\varepsilon=0$), to analyzing the effective disordered ring Hamiltonian, and finally deriving the curvature-dependent crossover law by comparing flat space, hyperbolic, and general constant-curvature regimes.
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous theoretical framework for understanding how geometric constraints (curvature) fundamentally alter localization physics in disordered quantum systems, which has implications for wave propagation in curved media or complex lattice structures.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Geometry and localization mechanisms. A random ra- dial potential first produces a mode whose envelope is localized around a geodesic radius r0 with radial localization length ξr. Exact rotational symmetry makes this mode extended around the associated circle. A weak angle-dependent perturbation then localizes the projected mode along the physical arc coordi- nate s, with angular localization length ξθ. The Poincar´e-disk edge is the conformal boundary at infinite geodesic distance, not a finite outer wall.

FIG. 2. Disorder-induced radial localization. (a) Radial Lyapunov exponent γr versus squared disorder width W 2 r . Symbols are infinite-half-line transfer-matrix results; the line is the Born approximation in Eq. (16). (b) Absolute finite-length rate |ΓR| for clean, periodic, and random radial potentials. The first two approach zero, while the random ensemble approaches a positive asymptotic rate. Error bars show standard errors where disorder averaging is used.

FIG. 3. Boundary-condition robustness of radially localized bulk states. (a) Median three-boundary energy spread ∆Ebc versus the boundary distance db measured in units of the inverse-participation length ξIPR. (b) Median core-density spread and matched-state overlap. Symbols summarize independent disorder realizations; bands or error bars indicate interquartile ranges. Straight lines in semilogarithmic coordinates are the fits in Eqs. (21) and (22).

FIG. 4. Angular localization of the projected shell. (a) Angular Lyapunov exponent γθ versus ε2. The displayed finite-window quadratic coefficient is 1.3% above the discrete Born value; its weak-disorder intercept is resolved independently in Fig. 9. (b) Normalized shell-extension indicator Qsh versus the one-parameter scaling variable L/ξθ. In the unit-spacing discretization L = N, so this is the same variable written as N/ξθ in the text. The common collapse demonstrates a circumference-controlled crossover.

FIG. 5. Extraction and geometric conversion of the shell crossover. (a) The vertical markers identify the hyperbolic crossover radii r∗obtained by converting the extracted circumferences N∗at which Qsh = 1/2. (b) The same N∗values converted to r∗in flat and hyperbolic geometry. The flat conversion grows algebraically as the perturbation weakens, while the hyperbolic conversion bends to the logarithmic law in Eq. (47).
